cases.name: grill-adr-worthy
cases.promptMarkdown:
/bg-skills:grill Plan for the order service rework. Three things are already decided:

1. Order storage moves from CRUD tables to an event-sourced log. We compared it with adding an audit table and with change data capture, and picked event sourcing because auditors must be able to replay any order's full history. Going back later would mean rebuilding every read model.
2. Orders stay in our existing Postgres cluster. It is the only database we run and nobody proposed anything else.
3. The "Export" button on the orders page gets relabelled "Download CSV".

Grill me on the rest of the plan.

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\user\Projects\BG-skills\.claude\worktrees\agent-a9b47f08329709d13\skills\productivity\grilling

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Answers to a round ("yes", "agree all", agreeing question by question) settle that round's questions; they never end the session. While any branch is open, the next step is the next round.

Once the frontier is empty, ask one closing question, on its own, not inside a round: have we reached a shared understanding? Take no action until the user answers it.

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\user\Projects\BG-skills\.claude\worktrees\agent-a9b47f08329709d13\skills\engineering\domain-modeling

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011CgrihwJD5Bw4PLGitJMQJ","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01Pd8Jpkp6YpcjxqRtAxj1se","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\claude-eval-2hnV3t\home\cwd\docs\adr\0001-event-sourced-orders.md","content":"# Orders are event-sourced

Order storage moves from CRUD tables to an append-only event log, because auditors must be able to replay any order's full history. Rebuilding state from the log is the source of truth; every read model is a projection of it, so reversing this decision would mean rebuilding every read model.

## Considered Options

❓ **Q1** - **What "replay" means for auditors**: There are three possible levels:
(a) Auditors can see the ordered list of events for an order.
(b) They can also rebuild the order's exact state at any past moment.
(c) They can also see *who* caused each change and *why* (actor, reason, source system).
(c) means every event needs required actor and cause metadata from day one, because you can't add it to old events later.

➡️ (c). Every event records the time it happened, the time it was recorded, the actor and the cause. Is that what the auditors need?

---

❓ **Q2** - **How big an event is**: Events can be business-level facts (`OrderPlaced`, `LineItemAdded`, `OrderCancelled`, `RefundIssued`) or generic `OrderUpdated { changedFields }` events. The generic kind is just CDC rebuilt by hand, which undercuts the reason you rejected CDC.

➡️ Business-level events only, named in past tense. A generic "updated" event is not allowed.

---

❓ **Q3** - **History of existing orders**: Today's CRUD rows hold current state only, with no history. At cutover, each existing order could:
(a) start its stream with one `OrderImported` snapshot event that is clearly marked as "history before this point unknown"
(b) get a history rebuilt from timestamps and logs that you guess at
(c) stay in the old tables, with only new orders event-sourced

➡️ (a). Auditors can tell real history from imported state, and nothing is made up. Will the auditors accept that pre-cutover orders can't be fully replayed?

---

❓ **Q4** - **Personal data in a log you can't change**: Orders contain customer names, addresses and so on. If an erasure request (e.g. GDPR) arrives, you can't edit past events without breaking replay. Options:
(a) Events hold only a customer ID, and personal data lives in a separate store you can edit.
(b) Personal data in events is encrypted with a key per customer, and erasing someone means destroying their key ("crypto-shredding").
(c) Erasure requests don't apply to you.

➡️ (a). It's the simplest, and the snapshot of the shipping address at order time goes in a separate store you can erase from.

---

➡️ The main orders read model is updated in the same transaction (both are in one Postgres cluster, so this is cheap). Background updates are used only for reporting and heavy read models.

---

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Answers to a round ("yes", "agree all", agreeing question by question) settle that round's questions; they never end the session. While any branch is open, the next step is the next round.

Once the frontier is empty, ask one closing question, on its own, not inside a round: have we reached a shared understanding? Take no action until the user answers it.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

None of the three is up for debate here. Round 1:

❓ **Q1** - **What an event looks like**: Events can record what happened in business terms (`OrderPlaced`, `LineAdded`, `ShippingAddressChanged`, `OrderCancelled`) or which fields changed (`OrderUpdated { fields… }`). Field-level events are quicker to write, but an auditor replaying them sees which columns changed, not what happened to the order or why.

➡️ Use business-intent events, named in the past tense. A generic `OrderUpdated` event isn't allowed.

---

❓ **Q2** - **Orders that already exist**: Orders placed before the cutover have no history to replay. Options:
(a) Give each existing order one `OrderImported` event that holds its current state. Its history starts at the cutover.
(b) Try to rebuild past events from logs or backups.
(c) Leave old orders in the CRUD tables, read-only, and only send new orders through the event log.

➡️ (a). Also tell the auditors in writing that history before the cutover is a snapshot, not a full replay. That way the "any order" promise isn't broken without anyone noticing.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Fixing mistakes**: An order gets the wrong price or the wrong customer. Do you fix it only by appending a correcting event (`PriceCorrected`, `OrderReassigned`), or can anyone ever edit or delete an event?

➡️ Only by appending a correcting event. Nobody edits or deletes events, not even admins, and this is enforced with database permissions on the events table.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Personal data and retention**: The log keeps everything forever, but customers can ask to have their data erased, and auditors need history kept for some fixed period. Do events hold personal data such as names, addresses and emails? And how long must history be kept?

➡️ Events refer to customers by ID only. Personal data stays in a mutable customer store that can be erased. The retention period comes from compliance; please give me the actual number.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Two edits to the same order at once**: Two people edit the same order at the same moment. Should the second write fail, with each event numbered within its order and a uniqueness check on that number, or should the last write win?

➡️ The second write fails and the caller retries. Last-write-wins quietly loses events, which defeats the point of the log.

---

❓ **Q6** - **How fresh the read models are**: The orders page and the CSV come from read models. Do you update them in the same Postgres transaction that appends the event, so they're always up to date, or in the background, so they can lag by a few seconds?

➡️ Same transaction for now. Everything is already in one Postgres, and it means a user never saves an order and then doesn't see the change. Switch a read model to background updates only when it's too slow to update inline.

---

❓ **Q7** - **Changing event formats later**: In a year `OrderPlaced` needs a new field. Do you convert old events to the new format when you read them and never rewrite stored events, or migrate the stored events in place?

➡️ Convert when reading. Stored events never change, because rewriting them would undermine the audit claim.

---

❓ **Q8** - **What "replay" means for auditors**: How do auditors actually see an order's history? Options: a history view in the app, an exported report per order, or direct read-only SQL access to the events table.

➡️ An order history view inside the app, showing each event with its time and who did it, plus an export of that same view. No direct database access.

---

❓ **Q9** - **What "Download CSV" exports**: Does the relabelled button export the current state of each order (what Export does today), or event history?

➡️ Current state from the read model, the same as today. Auditor history exports are a separate thing (Q8).

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\user\Projects\BG-skills\.claude\worktrees\agent-a9b47f08329709d13\skills\productivity\grilling

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Answers to a round ("yes", "agree all", agreeing question by question) settle that round's questions; they never end the session. While any branch is open, the next step is the next round.

Once the frontier is empty, ask one closing question, on its own, not inside a round: have we reached a shared understanding? Take no action until the user answers it.

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\user\Projects\BG-skills\.claude\worktrees\agent-a9b47f08329709d13\skills\engineering\domain-modeling

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

Auditors must be able to replay any order's full history, so order storage moves from CRUD tables to an event-sourced log. The event log is the source of truth, and every read model is a projection of it.

## Considered Options

- **Audit table next to the CRUD tables**: rejected. It records changes alongside the state, but the CRUD row is still the truth, so there's no guarantee a replay of the audit rows matches what the order actually was.
- **Change data capture on the CRUD tables**: rejected. It captures row-level diffs, not domain intent, and replaying it depends on the CDC pipeline never dropping or reordering anything.
- **Event sourcing**: chosen. The history *is* the order, so replay is exact by construction.

## Consequences

Auditors must be able to replay any order's full history, so order storage moves from CRUD tables to an event-sourced log. The event log is the source of truth, and every read model is a projection of it.

## Considered Options

- **Audit table next to the CRUD tables**: rejected. It records changes alongside the state, but the CRUD row is still the truth, so there's no guarantee a replay of the audit rows matches what the order actually was.
- **Change data capture on the CRUD tables**: rejected. It captures row-level diffs, not domain intent, and replaying it depends on the CDC pipeline never dropping or reordering anything.
- **Event sourcing**: chosen. The history *is* the order, so replay is exact by construction.

## Consequences

Going back to CRUD would mean rebuilding every read model, so treat this as effectively one-way.

Round 1. These questions depend only on what you've already decided:

---

❓ **Q1** - **What does "replay" mean to an auditor?**: "Replay any order's full history" could mean:
(a) a readable timeline of every event on an order: what happened, when and by whom;
(b) rebuilding the order as it stood at any past moment ("show me order 123 as of 3 March");
(c) both, plus proof that the log hasn't been tampered with (for example, hash-chained events).
Your answer decides what metadata each event must carry: who did it, when, and why.

➡️ (b), which also covers (a). Every event records who did it, when it happened and when it was recorded, plus an optional reason. Tamper evidence waits until an auditor actually asks for it.

---

❓ **Q2** - **What is the history of orders that existed before the migration?**: Orders created under CRUD have no event history, only their current state. Options:
(a) a single `OrderImported` event per order holding its state at migration time, so history starts at cutover;
(b) build fake history out of whatever timestamps and status columns exist;
(c) don't migrate them: old orders stay read-only in the legacy tables.

➡️ (a). Fake history would give auditors invented facts, which is worse than an honest gap. The import event should say plainly that earlier history wasn't recorded.

---

❓ **Q3** - **What is one event stream?**: Is the consistency boundary one stream per Order, with line items, payments and shipments as events inside it? Or do some of those get streams of their own?

➡️ One stream per Order, with line items inside it. Payments and shipments stay outside, and the Order only records facts about them (for example `PaymentCaptured`). That keeps each stream small and makes "replay this order" a single read.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Are read models updated in the same transaction as the event or afterwards?**: Since both live in the same Postgres cluster, you can project in the same transaction, so reads are always current. The alternative is an async projector, which reads lag slightly behind writes.

➡️ The orders-page read model, which drives the list and the CSV download, updates in the same transaction. Anything heavier, like reporting or search, runs async. Users should never see an order they just changed showing old data.

---

❓ **Q5** - **How do you fix mistakes when the log can't be edited?**: Someone records the wrong quantity or address. Options:
(a) only through compensating events (`OrderLineCorrected`) — nobody ever edits or deletes an event;
(b) allow an admin to amend events.

➡️ (a), with no exceptions. One edited event and the audit guarantee is worthless.

---

❓ **Q6** - **What happens with erasure requests when events are immutable?**: Orders hold personal data like names and addresses. When a customer asks to be erased under GDPR or a similar law, an immutable log conflicts with the request. Options:
(a) keep personal data out of events and store it in a separate table that can be deleted, referenced by ID;
(b) crypto-shredding: encrypt personal fields with a key per customer and delete the key;
(c) erasure doesn't apply here (for example, B2B only, or a legal retention period overrides it).

➡️ (a). It's the simplest approach and keeps the log clean. Unless (c) is true, in which case write it down as a constraint.

---

(a) big bang: freeze writes, import, switch;
(b) dual-write for a period, compare CRUD state against the event-sourced state, then switch.

I'm treating your three decisions as settled: event sourcing, Postgres, and the button label. The questions below are about everything else. They're ordered by how badly a wrong answer would hurt, so start at the top.

### Highest risk

**1. What happens to orders that already exist?**
Today's CRUD tables only hold current state, so older orders have no full history to replay. Your main reason for event sourcing is that auditors can replay any order's full history.
- Will you create a synthetic `OrderImported` starting event from current state? Or rebuild history from logs or backups?
- Have the auditors agreed that history before the cutover date can begin with a snapshot? If they haven't, the stated goal doesn't hold for every order that exists today.

**2. How do you cut over, and what's the rollback?**
You said going back means rebuilding every read model. So what is the plan if production breaks in week one?
- Big-bang switch, dual-write, or running the event log in shadow next to CRUD for a while?
- If you dual-write, which side is the source of truth while both run, and how do you detect when they disagree?

**3. Who reads the current order tables directly?**
Think of other services, BI or reporting jobs, finance exports, ad-hoc SQL, and the CSV download itself. Each one needs a read model or must be migrated. Do you have that list, and who owns each item on it?

**4. Personal data in an append-only log.**
Order events will contain names, addresses and maybe payment details. How will you handle erasure requests (GDPR or similar) when events can't change?
- Crypto-shredding with a per-customer key?
- Keeping personal data out of events and referencing it instead?
- Have legal and the auditors agreed that this approach still counts as "full history"?

### Design questions you'll hit in month one

**5. How are concurrent writes to the same order handled?**
Will you use optimistic concurrency, i.e. a unique key on `(stream_id, version)` and a check against the expected version? What does a caller see when a write conflicts: a retry or an error?

**6. Are read models updated in the same transaction or asynchronously?**
If asynchronously, how does the orders page handle someone who just changed an order and immediately reloads it? Who gets alerted when a projector stalls?

**7. How do event schemas change over time?**
Events are stored forever. When `OrderPlaced` gains a field next year, will you upcast old events on read, version the event types, or never change events and only add new ones? Who reviews changes to event schemas?

**8. How are mistakes corrected?**
If a bad event is written (a bug, or an operator error), do you fix it with a compensating event? Who has permission to issue one, and how does it show up for auditors?

**9. How do other systems learn about order changes?**
Will you use a transactional outbox, logical replication, or polling the event table? Do consumers need events in order per order, or globally?

### Operational details

**10. Volume and replay cost.**
How many events per order, and in total per year? Will you need snapshots? Will you partition the events table? How long does rebuilding a full read model take, and is that acceptable during an incident?

**11. Idempotency.**
Can commands be retried (by clients, queues or payment webhooks) without writing duplicate events?

**12. What does "done" mean?**
What are the success criteria, the deadline and the owner? Which part of the old CRUD path gets deleted, and when?

Answer 1–4 first. I'm treating your three decisions as fixed: event sourcing, Postgres, and the relabel. The questions below are about what those decisions leave open, starting with the riskiest.

### 1. Migrating existing orders
Your current CRUD tables only hold each order's latest state, not its history. Auditors are told they can replay "any order's full history."
- What happens to orders created before the cutover? Do you create one synthetic `OrderImported` event per order, or try to rebuild history from logs or backups?
- If it's a synthetic event, have the auditors agreed that history before the cutover date is just a snapshot? If they haven't, the main requirement fails for every existing order.

### 2. Deletion vs. an immutable log
- Do order events contain personal data (names, addresses, emails)? If so, how will you handle GDPR or similar erasure requests on a log that's supposed to be append-only?
- Options: keep personal data out of events and reference it by ID, encrypt it per customer and delete the key ("crypto-shredding"), or allow redacting events. Which one, and does Legal accept that it still counts as a full history?

### 3. Event store design in Postgres
- One `events` table with `(stream_id, version)` unique, plus a global sequence number? How will you stop two commands on the same order from both writing version N+1? A unique constraint is the minimum. Do you also want explicit expected-version checks?
- Postgres sequences can leave gaps and can commit out of order. If projections read by global position, how do you avoid skipping an event whose transaction commits late? (Common fixes: an outbox table, `pg_xact_commit_timestamp`, or a single writer per partition.)
- How fast do you expect the table to grow, and what's the plan for partitioning or retention? Retention is tricky when the auditors want everything.

### 4. Event schema evolution
- Events are kept forever, but your code will keep changing. How will you version event payloads: upcasters, a `schema_version` field, or never changing an event type once it ships?
- Who reviews new event types? An event named `OrderUpdated` with a diff payload would quietly turn this back into CRUD.

### 5. Read models and consistency
- Which read models do you need on day one? The orders page, CSV download, reporting, anything downstream?
- Are projections updated in the same transaction as the write, or asynchronously? If asynchronously, can the UI handle a user who doesn't see their change right after saving it?
- How long does a full projection rebuild take at today's volume? Rebuilding is your stated cost of going back, and it's also what you'll do every time a projection has a bug.

### 6. What "replay" means for auditors
- Do auditors need raw events, or the order's state as of a given time? Who builds that tool, and is it in scope for this rework?
- Do events record who acted and why (actor, causation/correlation IDs), or only what changed? Auditors usually care most about who.

### 7. Side effects and other consumers
- Which systems react to order changes today (payments, fulfilment, email)? Will they subscribe to events? If so, delivery is at-least-once, so are those handlers idempotent?
- When you replay events to rebuild a projection, what stops emails or charges from firing again?

### 8. Cutover and rollback
- Big-bang or dual-write? If dual-write, which side is the source of truth while both run, and how do you detect drift?
- Your answer to #1 makes going back expensive. What exactly is the rollback plan for the first two weeks after launch?

### 9. "Download CSV"
The label is settled. The open question is the data behind it: will it read from a projection? And will the columns stay exactly the same, so nobody's spreadsheets or scripts break during the migration?

---

**2. Event schema and versioning**
- Events are permanent. How will you handle a change to an event's shape? Upcasting on read, versioned event types, or never changing events at all?

- How will two writers be stopped from appending to the same order at once? Optimistic concurrency on a per-stream version number with a unique constraint `(stream_id, version)`?
- Which reads have to see a write immediately (for example, a user's own order page right after checkout)? And which can tolerate projection lag?
- Do any invariants span more than one order, such as stock reservations or per-customer limits? Event sourcing per order won't enforce those for you.

**4. Read models and projections**
- Which read models will you need at launch? The orders list, the order detail page, the CSV download, reporting?
- Will projections update synchronously in the same transaction as the append, or asynchronously? If asynchronously, how do they find new events: polling a global sequence, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, or an outbox?
- Global ordering in Postgres has a known trap: transactions can commit out of sequence order, so a poller can skip events. How will you handle that?
- How long does a full rebuild of a projection take at today's volume, and at 10× that volume? Can you rebuild without downtime, for example by building a new table and then swapping it in?

- Event tables grow forever. What's the expected growth? Will you partition the table, and what's the plan for vacuum and index bloat?
- Will snapshots be used for orders with long histories, and what triggers taking one?

cases.name: grill-small-feature
cases.promptMarkdown: /bg-skills:grill I want to add CSV export to the orders page of our internal admin app. Staff click a button and get a file of the orders currently shown. That is the whole idea so far.

graders.name: whole-frontier
graders.graderMarkdown:

PASS if the reply asks at least three questions about separate open decisions in this one round, each question is numbered, and each question has its own recommended answer. It does not need to say "waiting for your answers" explicitly.

graders.evidence:
The working directory is empty: no code, no `GLOSSARY.md`, no ADRs. So I can't check anything against an existing model, and every question below goes to you. Round 1 covers the decisions that don't depend on anything else.

❓ **Q1** - **What "orders currently shown" means**: The orders page probably has filters, sorting and pagination. "Currently shown" could mean:
- (a) only the rows on the current page (say 25 of 3,000)
- (b) every order that matches the current filters and sort, across all pages
- (c) every order, ignoring filters

Staff almost always want (b) and are surprised when they get (a). But (b) means the export can be very large.

➡️ (b): every order matching the active filters and sort, across all pages. I'd call this an **Order Export** of the current **Order View** (filters + sort, no pagination).

---

❓ **Q2** - **One row per order, or per line item**: Does each CSV row represent one Order (with totals), or one line item within an order (order fields repeated on each line)? Line-item rows are better for analysis but don't match what the page shows.

➡️ One row per Order, matching the page. A line-item export would be a separate feature later if anyone asks for it.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Which columns**: Should the CSV:
- (a) mirror the columns visible on the page, including any the user has hidden or reordered
- (b) use a fixed, documented set of columns that may include fields the page doesn't show (internal IDs, raw timestamps, etc.)

Option (a) gives "what you see is what you get". Option (b) gives files that downstream spreadsheets and scripts can depend on.

➡️ (b): a fixed column set, a superset of the page's default columns, in a stable order. People who export usually feed the file into something else, and that something breaks when columns move.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Who can export**: Orders usually contain customer personal data (names, emails, addresses). A CSV is a copy that leaves the app and can't be revoked. Can everyone who can view the orders page export, or only a specific role or permission?

➡️ A separate export permission, granted to a subset of the staff who can view orders. Viewing data and taking a portable copy of it carry different risks.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Audit trail**: Should every export be recorded (who, when, which filters, how many rows)?

➡️ Yes. It's cheap, and it's the first thing anyone will ask for if a file leaks.

---

Once these are settled, the next round covers size limits and sync vs. async delivery (depends on Q1), plus formatting details: timezones, money, Excel quirks, and formula injection (depends on Q3).

graders.evidence:
I looked for the admin app's code first, but the working directory (`…\home\cwd`) is an empty repo with no code and no `GLOSSARY.md`. So I can't check your answers against how orders are actually modelled. If the app is somewhere else, tell me the path and I'll check things there myself rather than asking you.

Round 1 covers the decisions that don't depend on anything else yet.

---

❓ **Q1** - **What does "orders currently shown" mean?** The orders page probably has filters, sorting and pagination. "Currently shown" could mean:
- (a) **just the visible page**, e.g. the 50 rows on screen
- (b) **every order matching the current filters and sort**, across all pages
- (c) every order, ignoring filters

Staff who say "export what I'm looking at" almost always mean (b). Option (a) catches people out when they get 50 rows and expected 3,000.

➡️ (b): every order matching the current filters, in the current sort order, ignoring pagination.

---

❓ **Q2** - **What does one CSV row represent?** If an order has several line items, a row can be:
- (a) **one order** per row, with order-level fields only (totals, status, customer, dates)
- (b) **one line item** per row, with the order fields repeated on each row
- (c) one order per row, with line items squashed into a single cell

➡️ (a): one row per order. Line-item exports are a different feature with different users, and we can add them later.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Which columns go in the file?**
- (a) **the same columns as the on-screen table**, in the same order
- (b) **a fixed, fuller set of export columns**, for example internal IDs, raw timestamps and amounts without currency formatting
- (c) columns staff pick at export time

➡️ (b): a fixed export column set that is the visible columns plus the IDs and raw values people need for spreadsheets. Values are unformatted: ISO 8601 timestamps with timezone, and decimal amounts with a separate currency column.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Who is allowed to export?** A bulk export lets someone take customer personal data (names, addresses, emails) out of the app in one file. Viewing a page doesn't. Choices:
- (a) anyone who can see the orders page
- (b) only staff given a separate **export permission**

➡️ (b): a separate export permission. Exporting is a different level of risk from viewing, and a separate permission lets you give it out narrowly.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Should exports be recorded?** Should each export log who ran it, when, which filters were applied and how many rows came out?

➡️ Yes. Keep an audit record for every export. It's cheap, and it's what you'll want the first time someone asks "who pulled all the customer data last month?"

---

❓ **Q6** - **Which spreadsheet tool should the file work best in?** Excel mangles plain UTF-8 CSVs (accented names break, long IDs turn into scientific notation, leading zeros vanish). It also runs cells that start with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` as formulas, which is a known injection risk.

➡️ Target Excel. Write UTF-8 with a BOM, comma delimiters and full quoting, and escape cells that start with formula characters.

---

❓ **Q7** - **What should the file be called?**

➡️ `orders-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.csv`, using the export time in UTC.

---

Once these are settled, the next round will cover the questions that depend on them: how large an export can get and whether it runs instantly or in the background (depends on Q1), and whether "order" needs a precise glossary definition (depends on Q2). "The orders currently shown" carries most of the weight in your idea, so most of the questions start there.

### 1. What does "currently shown" mean?

- **What if the data changes between viewing and clicking?** New orders arrive all the time. Is "as of the click" acceptable?

### 2. How big can it get?
- **What's the biggest realistic export?** 500 rows, 50k, or 2M? This decides the design:
  - Small: build it synchronously in the request and stream the response.
  - Large: run a background job and send a link or notification when it's ready. You'd also need timeouts, memory limits and a "your export is ready" flow.
- **Is there a cap?** If someone exports with no filters, what should happen?

### 3. Which columns?
- **Is it exactly the visible table columns, or a fixed "export schema"?** Visible columns usually leave out what people actually want, like line items, customer email, addresses, tax and refunds.
- **Line items:** one row per order or one row per line item? This choice matters more than any other column decision.
- **Formats:** money as `12.50` or `$12.50`? Which currency? Dates in UTC or the staff member's timezone, and in ISO format? Status as internal enum or display label?

### 4. Who's allowed, and what leaks?
- **Can every admin user export, or only some roles?** Viewing 25 orders on screen is very different from downloading 50k customers' PII.
- **Does the export contain PII** (names, emails, addresses, phone numbers)? If so, do you need audit logging of who exported what and when, and are there GDPR or retention concerns once the file leaves your system?
- **Is the export endpoint authorized the same way the page is?** Or could someone call it with modified filters to get orders they can't see in the UI, for example from other stores or tenants?

### 5. CSV gotchas
- **CSV/formula injection:** a customer named `=HYPERLINK(...)` will execute when staff open the file in Excel. Values starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` need escaping.
- **Excel compatibility:** add a UTF-8 BOM so accented names display correctly. Quote commas, quotes and newlines (notes fields often contain them). Decide on a delimiter if you have European staff whose Excel expects `;`.
- **Filename:** something like `orders-2026-11-08-filtered.csv`?

### 6. What problem is this solving?
- **What do staff do with the file?** Reconciliation in Excel, sending it to accounting, importing it elsewhere? If it's feeding another system, an exact, stable column contract matters more than readability. If it's one recurring report, a scheduled report might be the better feature.

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Answers to a round ("yes", "agree all", agreeing question by question) settle that round's questions; they never end the session. While any branch is open, the next step is the next round.

Once the frontier is empty, ask one closing question, on its own, not inside a round: have we reached a shared understanding? Take no action until the user answers it.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

graders.evidence:
# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them until delivery.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

**Cancellation**:
Withdrawing an entire Order before Dispatch, so nothing is sent and nothing is charged.
_Avoid_: Void, abort

**Return**:
A customer sending back one delivered Line Item from an Order to be refunded for that Line Item alone. The rest of the Order is unaffected.
_Avoid_: Cancel an item, partial cancellation, item cancellation

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\user\Projects\BG-skills\.claude\worktrees\agent-a9b47f08329709d13\skills\productivity\grilling

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Answers to a round ("yes", "agree all", agreeing question by question) settle that round's questions; they never end the session. While any branch is open, the next step is the next round.

Once the frontier is empty, ask one closing question, on its own, not inside a round: have we reached a shared understanding? Take no action until the user answers it.

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\user\Projects\BG-skills\.claude\worktrees\agent-a9b47f08329709d13\skills\engineering\domain-modeling

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

","originalFile":"# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them until delivery.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

graders.name: glossary-written-inline
graders.evidence:
# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them until delivery.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

**Cancellation**:
Withdrawing an entire Order before Dispatch, so nothing is sent and nothing is charged.
_Avoid_: Void, abort

**Return**:
A customer sending back a single delivered Line Item, refunded for that Line Item only.
_Avoid_: Item cancellation, partial cancellation, cancelling an item

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Answers to a round ("yes", "agree all", agreeing question by question) settle that round's questions; they never end the session. While any branch is open, the next step is the next round.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

➡️ Yes, a Return covers some or all of a Line Item's delivered quantity. It's still one Line Item per Return, but customers expect to send back one broken mug without returning the other two.

---

❓ **Q2** - **One Line Item per Return**: If a customer wants to send back two different Line Items from the same Order, do they open two separate Returns? Should one Return always mean exactly one Line Item?

---

❓ **Q3** - **What counts as "arrived"**: The glossary has **Dispatch** (leaves the warehouse) but no term for arrival. Should I add **Delivery** ("the moment a Line Item reaches the customer") and make it the event that makes a Line Item returnable? Should it be tracked per Line Item rather than per Order, so split parcels work?

➡️ Yes, add **Delivery**, tracked per Line Item. A Return becomes possible once that Line Item is delivered, even if other parts of the Order are still on their way.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Between Dispatch and Delivery**: Cancellation stops at Dispatch and a Return only starts at Delivery. ➡️ Yes, they wait and make a Return. There's no in-transit mechanism for now.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Return window**: Should there be a time limit after Delivery for starting a Return, set at 30 days?

➡️ Yes, 30 days from that Line Item's Delivery.

---

❓ **Q6** - **When the refund happens**: Should the refund be issued only after the warehouse receives and checks the returned item? The alternatives are refunding when the customer requests the Return, or when the carrier scans the parcel.

➡️ Yes, refund when the warehouse receives and accepts the item.

---

❓ **Q7** - **Refund amount**: Should the refund be what the customer actually paid for the returned units? That means the unit price minus their share of any Order-level discount, with the original delivery charge not refunded.

➡️ Yes, refund the amount paid for the returned units, with Order-level discounts split across Line Items in proportion to price. Original shipping is not refunded.

➡️ Yes, a reason is required. Later questions about return shipping costs and checking items will depend on it.

graders.evidence:
# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them until delivery.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

**Cancellation**:
Withdrawing an entire Order before Dispatch, so nothing is sent and nothing is charged.
_Avoid_: Void, abort

**Return**:
A customer sending back one delivered Line Item and receiving a refund for that Line Item only. The rest of the Order is unaffected.
_Avoid_: Item cancellation, cancel an item, partial cancellation, RMA

graders.evidence:
# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them through delivery and any Returns.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

**Cancellation**:
Withdrawing an entire Order before Dispatch, so nothing is sent and nothing is charged.
Applies only to whole Orders and only before Dispatch; sending back a delivered Line Item is a **Return**, not a Cancellation.
_Avoid_: Void, abort

**Return**:
A customer sending back one delivered Line Item and receiving a Refund for that Line Item only. The rest of the Order is unaffected.
_Avoid_: Cancel an item, item cancellation, partial cancellation

**Refund**:
Money paid back to the customer for a Returned Line Item, limited to what was charged for that Line Item.
_Avoid_: Reimbursement, credit

graders.evidence:
# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them through delivery and any returns.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

**Cancellation**:
Withdrawing an entire Order before Dispatch, so nothing is sent and nothing is charged.
Applies only to whole Orders before Dispatch; a delivered Line Item coming back is a Return.
_Avoid_: Void, abort

**Return**:
A customer sending back a single delivered Line Item and being refunded for that Line Item only. The rest of the Order is unaffected.
_Avoid_: Cancel an item, item cancellation, partial cancellation

# Ordering

How customers place orders and how the shop handles them until delivery.

## Language

**Order**:
A customer's request to buy one or more items, placed in a single checkout.
_Avoid_: Purchase, basket

**Line Item**:
One product and its quantity within an Order.
_Avoid_: Order line, entry

**Dispatch**:
The moment an Order leaves the warehouse.
_Avoid_: Shipping, fulfilment

**Cancellation**:
Withdrawing an entire Order before Dispatch, so nothing is sent and nothing is charged.
_Avoid_: Void, abort

**Return**:
A customer sending back a single delivered Line Item and getting a refund for that Line Item only. The rest of the Order is not affected. Only possible after the Order has arrived. Not a Cancellation, which covers a whole Order before Dispatch.
_Avoid_: Cancel an item, item cancellation, partial cancellation
